question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

2.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. The statement holds because a polygenic score is constructed as a finite weighted sum of estimated SNP effects; even in the absence of population stratification or other biases, sampling error and imperfect tagging mean that the realized variance explained by the score is always strictly less than the total SNP heritability (which reflects the sum of all causal and tagged variant effects in the population). Only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly measured data would equality be possible, but that limit is never attained in practice.

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by the additive effects of all SNPs (i.e., the variance of the latent genetic score \(G\)). A polygenic score is a finite-sample linear predictor \(\hat{G} = X\hat{\beta}\) whose weights \(\hat{\beta}\) are estimated from the same or an independent GWAS. Because of sampling error, imperfect LD tagging, winner’s curse, and the need for regularization, \(\text{Var}(\hat{G})\) and \(\text{Cov}(\hat{G},Y)\) are strictly smaller than their population counterparts; hence the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any practicable PGS is necessarily lower than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Equality is attained only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained samples, which is never realized in practice.

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is tagged by (and could, in principle, be recovered from) the set of SNPs. A polygenic score is a finite-sample linear predictor whose weights are noisy estimates of the true SNP effects. Because those weights contain estimation error, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any PGS is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\) (except in the theoretical limit of infinite discovery-sample size, which is never attained in practice). Consequently the statement is true.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True, because a polygenic score is constructed from estimated effect sizes (typically via GWAS or a regularized model like PRS-CS or LDpred), which necessarily contain sampling noise and incomplete tagging of causal variants; even in the absence of environmental effects, these imperfections mean the out-of-sample variance explained by the score will fall short of the SNP-based heritability estimated in the same population.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is additively explained by all SNPs (i.e., the theoretical upper bound attainable if every SNP effect were known without error). A polygenic score, by contrast, is constructed from finite-sample effect-size estimates; the resulting out-of-sample \(R^2\) is therefore strictly attenuated by estimation error, imperfect LD tagging, winner’s-curse bias, and possible shrinkage or pruning steps. Equality between PGS \(R^2\) and \(h^2_{SNP}\) is reached only in the unattainable limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained data, so the inequality is necessarily strict in any real analysis.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the theoretical maximum proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by the optimal linear combination of all measured SNPs (i.e., the population-level best linear predictor). A polygenic score (PGS) is a specific linear predictor whose SNP weights are estimated from finite GWAS data. Because those weights contain sampling error, shrinkage, incomplete SNP coverage, and possible mismatch between discovery and target samples, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any PGS is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\) except in the idealized limit of infinite, perfectly harmonized data. Hence the predictive ability of a PGS is necessarily lower than SNP heritability.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance jointly explained by all SNPs (i.e., the population value of the coefficient of determination from the multiple regression of the phenotype on the full SNP matrix). A polygenic score is a linear predictor whose weights are estimated from finite data; even under ideal conditions (perfect LD, no stratification, optimal shrinkage), the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of any such score is bounded above by \(h^2_{SNP}\) and equals that bound only in the infinite-sample limit. Hence the predictive \(R^2\) is necessarily strictly lower than SNP heritability in any real analysis.

8.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. The SNP heritability captures the total additive genetic variance tagged by all measured SNPs, but a polygenic score is built from finite-sample effect-size estimates that are noisy, incomplete (owing to LD pruning, p-value thresholds, or regularization), and subject to winner’s curse; consequently the out-of-sample R² achieved by the score is invariably smaller than the SNP-heritability benchmark.

9.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by all measured SNPs together. A polygenic score, however, is a weighted sum of a finite, usually pruned or thresholded set of SNPs whose effect sizes are estimated with error in finite samples. Because of incomplete tagging, winner’s curse, and the need for regularization to avoid overfitting, the out-of-sample R² achieved by any practical PGS is therefore strictly lower than the SNP-heritability ceiling.

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability represents the total phenotypic variance that can be explained by an optimal linear combination of all measured SNPs (i.e., the theoretical upper bound for any linear predictor built from those SNPs). A polygenic score, however, is constructed from finite data: effect-size estimates are noisy, tagging is imperfect, and typically only a subset of SNPs is retained or weighted. Consequently its out-of-sample R² is strictly bounded above by the SNP heritability and, under any realistic sample size, falls below that bound. Equality is attainable only in the unattainable limit of infinite, perfectly genotyped data; hence the predictive ability “is necessarily lower.”

13.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be attributed to all SNPs in aggregate (typically estimated via methods like GREML or LD score regression). A polygenic score, by contrast, is a weighted sum of a finite number of SNPs whose effect sizes have been estimated from a discovery sample; even when the score is optimally constructed, the finite sample size, imperfect tagging of causal variants, and the need for regularization or pruning inevitably introduce shrinkage and noise. As a result, the out-of-sample variance explained by the score is bounded above by the SNP heritability and is therefore necessarily lower.

11.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance captured by the best linear combination of the observed SNPs (i.e., the additive variance tagged by the SNP panel). A polygenic score is precisely an estimate of that same linear predictor. Consequently, in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained training data drawn from the same population, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of the PGS equals \(h^2_{SNP}\). In finite samples the realized \(R^2\) is smaller because of estimation error, but the inequality is not strict by definition; the statement therefore does not hold.

12.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP-based heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by an optimal linear combination of the SNPs (i.e., the theoretical upper bound attainable by any additive predictor built from those markers). A polygenic score is simply one such linear predictor whose weights are estimated from finite data; with sufficiently large samples, perfect linkage-disequilibrium information, and appropriate shrinkage, its out-of-sample \(R^2\) can asymptotically reach (but not exceed) \(h^2_{SNP}\). Consequently the predictive ability is bounded above by SNP heritability, yet it is not necessarily strictly lower.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. The statement holds because a polygenic score is always constructed from finite GWAS summary statistics that include sampling noise, imperfect LD tagging, and winner's-curse effects; even in the theoretical limit these sources of attenuation ensure the out-of-sample R² cannot reach the full SNP-heritability ceiling.

15.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability represents the total variance in a phenotype that can be explained by SNPs (i.e., the performance of the optimal linear predictor given all SNPs). A polygenic score is a finite-sample estimate of that predictor; because the SNP effect sizes must be estimated rather than known exactly, the out-of-sample R² achieved by any PGS is strictly less than the SNP heritability (approaching equality only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained data). Hence the predictive ability is necessarily lower.

(The statement would be false only if “polygenic score” were redefined to mean the oracle predictor with known population weights, which is not the conventional usage.)

16.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

SNP heritability represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by additive effects of all SNPs (i.e., the performance of the optimal linear predictor). A polygenic score is itself a linear predictor formed from SNP effect sizes, so in the theoretical limit of perfect effect-size estimates its out-of-sample R² can equal (but not exceed) SNP heritability. The statement therefore claims something that is not necessarily true.

17.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The maximum out-of-sample R² attainable by a PGS equals (but does not exceed) SNP heritability when every SNP is included and its true effect size is known; finite-sample estimation error, imperfect tagging, or pruning therefore make observed R² lower in practice, but the inequality is not logically necessary.
